extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent practitioners, and stakeholders submitting comments to the USPTO on subject matter eligibility guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a claim element (or combination of elements) represents well-understood, routine, conventional activity for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 101 subject-matter eligibility (Mayo–Alice framework), as implemented in the USPTO's Berkheimer memorandum and related MPEP revisions. Applies to examination practice including formulation of rejections and evaluation of applicant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual nature of conventionality determination (Berkheimer)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whether something is well-understood, routine, and conventional to a skilled artisan at the time of the patent is a factual determination." (Berkheimer v. HP Inc., 881 F.3d 1360 (Fed. Cir. 2018))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Berkheimer decision makes clear that the question of whether claim limitations represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity raises disputed factual issues and cannot be resolved without appropriate factual support. Examiners must base such conclusions on factual findings supported as discussed in the Berkheimer memorandum and MPEP updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for concluding an element is well-understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: "An examiner should conclude that an element (or combination of elements) represents well-understood, routine, conventional activity only when the examiner can readily conclude that the element(s) is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry." (MPEP § 2106.05(d)(I))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conclusion that an element is conventional requires that it be shown to be widely prevalent or commonly used in the relevant field — not merely present in prior art. The examiner must be able to 'readily conclude' widespread prevalence and must support that conclusion in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality analysis parallels 35 U.S.C. 112(a) enablement/description analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Berkheimer memorandum specifies that "the analysis for determining whether an element (or combination of elements) is widely prevalent or in common use is the same as the analysis under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as to whether an element is so well-known that it need not be described in detail in the patent specification."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an element is so well-known that a specification need not describe it to satisfy 112(a), that same factual showing can support a determination that the element is well-understood, routine, conventional for 101 purposes. Conversely, absence of description in the specification alone does not establish conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from novelty/obviousness (35 U.S.C. 102/103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing that additional elements are obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, or lack novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102, is not by itself sufficient to establish that the additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities or elements to those in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere fact that something is disclosed in prior art does not mean it was well-understood, routine, and conventional; conventionality goes beyond mere disclosure in a document and concerns whether the activity/elements were widely prevalent or in common use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating rejections — required written support (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a step 2B analysis, an additional element (or combination of elements) is not well-understood, routine or conventional unless the examiner finds, and expressly supports a rejection in writing with, one or more of the following (items 1–4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must use one or more of the enumerated bases (specification/applicant statement; court decisions; publications; official notice) to support a 2B conventionality finding, and the rejection must be expressly supported in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support option 1: citation to specification or applicant statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A citation to an express statement in the specification or to a statement made by an applicant during prosecution that demonstrates the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification can demonstrate conventionality if it describes the additional elements as well-understood, routine or conventional (or equivalent), as a commercially-available product, or in a manner indicating the elements are sufficiently well-known that particulars need not be described to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a). A finding cannot be based solely on the specification being silent about the element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support option 2: citation to judicial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A citation to one or more of the court decisions discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(d)(II) as noting the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior court decisions that expressly recognize an element as well-understood or conventional may be cited to support a conventionality finding. The decision(s) cited should clearly indicate the conventional nature of the element in the relevant field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support option 3: citation to publications showing widespread prevalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A citation to a publication that demonstrates the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s) (e.g., book, manual, review article, or other source that describes the state of the art and what is well-known and in common use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all 'printed publications' under 35 U.S.C. 102 will suffice — the publication must demonstrate that the element(s) are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field, comparable to activities/elements so well-known that they need not be described in a patent application to satisfy 112(a). A single patent or a lone thesis placed in a library is generally insufficient unless it demonstrates widespread prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support option 4: examiner taking official notice (limited use)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement that the examiner is taking official notice of the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This option should be used only when the examiner is certain, based upon personal knowledge, that the additional elements are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field. Procedures for taking official notice and addressing applicant challenges are in MPEP § 2144.03; if challenged, the examiner must later provide evidentiary support (see evaluation of responses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on basing a finding solely on specification silence
rubrics_metrics.description: "A finding that an element is well-understood, routine, or conventional cannot be based only on the fact that the specification is silent with respect to describing such element."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silence in the specification does not equate to conventionality. Examiners must rely on affirmative evidence (spec disclosure, publications, court decisions, or official notice supported by personal knowledge) rather than mere absence of description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and scope of publications used as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A document may be a 'printed publication' for 102 purposes but still fail to establish that something it describes is well-understood, routine, conventional activity; the nature of the publication and its description must demonstrate widespread prevalence or common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a single patent or a lone foreign thesis may be a printed publication but typically do not alone demonstrate that the item was widely prevalent or commonly used. The publication(s) must be of a type and content that show community-wide practice or common usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating applicant's response when conventionality is challenged
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant challenges the examiner's position that the additional element(s) is well-understood, routine, conventional activity, the examiner should reevaluate whether it is readily apparent that the additional elements are in fact well-understood, routine, conventional activities to those in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner had taken official notice and the applicant specifically challenges that position, the examiner must then provide one of the evidentiary items discussed in support options 1–3, or an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.104(d)(2) setting forth specific factual statements and explanation to support the examiner's position.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP procedural updates to reflect Berkheimer (§§ 2106.07(a), 2106.07(b), 2106.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Berkheimer memorandum revises the procedures set forth in MPEP § 2106.07(a) (Formulating a Rejection For Lack of Subject Matter Eligibility) and MPEP § 2106.07(b) (Evaluating Applicant’s Response); MPEP § 2106.05(d)(I) guidance reiterated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP will be updated to incorporate these changes; examiners and practitioners should follow the revised procedures for formulating 2B rejections and for handling applicant responses and challenges.
